narrative:
The model estimates a 59% chance that you will fail your final year. That means you are more likely than not to fall short, so the school is treating additional remedial courses as required support. This is a warning signal, not a fixed outcome.

The strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure is your stated intention not to continue into higher education. Among students who passed, every one said they wanted higher education, so your answer stands out sharply. The second most influential factor works in your favor: you have no past class failures, which is typical of passers and lowers your risk. The third factor pushes you back toward failure: you study less than two hours per week. Only about one in five passers studied that little, while more than half studied two to five hours.

To improve, talk with a counselor about your plans after school and whether higher education is possible, and clarify the goals and steps required. Build a weekly study routine that raises study time to at least two to five hours, using school or family help. Review your very high going-out pattern and consider whether it is crowding out study time. Use the remedial courses to address these gaps early.
